source.snippet: Having sat in a trading seat at a GS competitor, I can second this. If a Claude Max subscription led to one better trade over the course of a year, there's an almost 100% chance that it would pay for itself. And consider that a trader at GS would be doing dozens if not thousands of trades per day... Cost isn't the issue here.

problem_statement: Financial institutions (banks, trading desks) are pulling AI coding and analysis tools from professional employees not due to cost but due to unresolved compliance, data-leakage, and audit-trail concerns — leaving high-value users without productivity tools they'd willingly pay for.
target_segment: Compliance and IT leadership at mid-to-large financial institutions (banks, hedge funds, trading desks) deploying or evaluating AI productivity tools for regulated staff.
notes: HN thread discusses Goldman Sachs pulling Claude Code from bankers and traders (2026-11-09, 11 points on related thread). Commenter with direct trading-seat experience frames the ROI clearly: even one better trade per year justifies the cost. The barrier is compliance/data risk, not price. This is a classic enterprise wedge: institutions want the tool but cannot clear legal/compliance review. A compliant, on-prem or VPC-deployed AI coding/analysis layer with audit logs, data-residency guarantees, and policy controls could command significant enterprise contract value. Explicit willingness-to-pay signal from the finance domain.
